## Exact assumptions and conditional bounds

- [`sat26-sparse`](../../ASSUMPTIONS.md#sat26-sparse)
- [`sat26-reported-formal`](../../ASSUMPTIONS.md#sat26-reported-formal)

Conditional on `sat26-sparse`:

$$
2^{O(m/\sqrt{\log m})}L^{O(1)}
$$

Alternatively, conditional on `sat26-reported-formal`:

$$
2^{O(m(\log\log m)^2/\sqrt{\log m})}L^{O(1)}
$$

The resulting algorithm is deterministic and uses polynomial space, conditional on the corresponding assumption and this derivation. $L$ denotes the original input length; constants may depend on the stated fixed constants. Logarithms in asymptotic bounds may be regularized when the declared measure is small.

## Preprocessing

If n=0, return one. If n>0 and an isolated vertex exists, return zero. Otherwise the active vertex count is at most 2m.

## Encoding size

| Quantity | Bound |
| --- | --- |
| Boolean variables, including auxiliaries | $O(m)$ |
| Clauses | $O(m)$ |
| Maximum clause width | $3$ |

## Derivation

1. Use one selection bit per edge. At every vertex, a linear-size counting circuit requires exactly one incident edge to be selected.

2. The sum of all vertex degrees is 2m, so the circuits and their bidirectional gate encodings have O(m) variables and clauses. Each selected edge set extends uniquely to gate values.

3. Apply the sparse counting assumption. Small m is handled directly; asymptotically the bound is B(m) times a polynomial in the full input length.

## Caveats and comparison limits

- Corollary 1.3 states 2^{o(n+m)}; removing the isolated-vertex cases gives the displayed edge-measure refinement.
- A 0–1 matrix permanent is the bipartite special case. For a dense t×t matrix, m=Θ(t²); this route does not establish 2^{o(t)} time.
- No arbitrary-weight permanent is claimed.

Counting requires a count-preserving encoding and preprocessing, or an explicit correction for multiplicities. The derivation must justify this; decision preservation alone is insufficient.

## Comparison with known results

`classical-benchmark-only` — For the bipartite 0–1 case, Ryser’s formula is a classical $2^t\operatorname{poly}(t)$ bit-time benchmark for t×t matrices. The new guarantee B(m) is subexponential in t when m=O(t), but the substitution m=Θ(t²) gives no improvement over that benchmark. This is not a claim about the latest best bound.

- **`servedio-wan2005`** — [Rocco A. Servedio and Andrew Wan, Computing sparse permanents faster](https://www.cs.columbia.edu/~atw12/papers/perm.pdf). Version: Author manuscript dated 18 June 2005. Locator: Section 2, page 3: Θ(t·2^t) arithmetic operations; 0–1 inputs have polynomial intermediate bit lengths.
